title: Head of Network Development
description:
HEAD OF NETWORK DEVELOPMENT Location Global, whereHelpAge can currently employ: Ethiopia, India, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, Nepal, Pakistan, Spain, Tanzania, Thailand, Turkey, United Kingdom or Zimbabwe, with a preference for candidates based in the Global South. Department Network Development Reports to (Line Manager) Director of Global Impact Responsible for (Line managing) Regional Advisers (4) Network SupportLead Humanitarian Capacity Strengthening Manager ( SHAPE ) Network Platform Manager SCORE Programme Manager Indirectly responsible for Country Director – Ukraine (viathe Network Support Lead) Grade F Contract Type Full time equivalent /Open-ended contract About HelpAge HelpAge International works with a diverse global network of around 200 organisations across 99 countries to promote the rights of older people to lead dignified, healthy and secure lives. Through partnership and collaborations, we work to ensure the inclusion of older people across society and strive to deliver a just and fair world for everyone as they get older. Our work is driven by our desire to achieve real impact for older people, to be inclusive, to work in partnership and to learn from our shared experience. As countries prepare for and adapt to population ageing, we are seeking to make a difference at a critical juncture to how societies, economies and institutions adapt to this change. Our Strategy 2030, Ageing in a Just World, sets out how we will work to shape the future we all share. By working together with our partners, we aim to inspire a movement for change. By ensuring all our work promotes older people’s wellbeing, dignity and voice, we seek to transform the lives of older people now and in the future. Guided by our commitment to our values of impact, learning, partnership, and inclusion, we partner with others to bring systemic change and impact at scale. By acting as a supporter, convenor and thought leader, we want to make an impact that matters for older people and their communities. Our organisational culture The culture of the organisation aims to ensure: Accountability for All: Every individual and team member is responsible for their actions and decisions, ensuring alignment with organisational priorities and commitments to partners and network members. Trust, Respect, and Inclusion: We strive to create an environment where mutual trust is the foundation of all relationships, diverse perspectives are valued, and everyone feels included in decision-making processes. Culture of Collaboration: Working together across teams, network members, and partners to share knowledge, maximise impact, and drive collective success, rather than working in silos. Openness and Transparency: Ensuring open communication, clear decision-making processes and actions, and a commitment to sharing information in a way that builds trust and accountability. Collective Responsibilities Within and With Partners and Network: Recognising that achieving our mission requires shared responsibility, we promote joint ownership of decisions, initiatives, and outcomes across HelpAge and its network members and partners. Staff and network members are valued: Staff and network members are recognised, and valued and appreciated for their contributions, fostering an environment where every individual feels respected, supported, and integral to our mission, with their input and expertise recognised as vital to achieving our shared goals. The Behavioural competencies outlined below support this culture. About the Department The Global Impact Team drives HelpAge International’s mission to advance the wellbeing, dignity, and rights of older people, by championing locally led action and global solidarity. At the heart of our work is a thriving, resilient HelpAge global network—a powerful collective of national civil society actors driving change that is rooted in the priorities and experiences of older people. We lead the delivery of HelpAge’s strategic approach to support, convene, and influence, across humanitarian and development contexts, to achieve lasting and inclusive impact. Our goal is to ensure that: Older people have inclusive, improved access to secure and adequate income Older people have safe and secure access to humanitarian assistance Older people have improved access to inclusive health, care, and support services Age-inclusive laws, policies and systems guarantee older people’s rights across all sectors A thriving locally led HelpAge Network drives collective action to uphold older people’s rights, dignity, and wellbeing. About the Job The Head of Network Development will provide strategic leadership for HelpAge International's global network engagement and development, localisation, and capacity strengthening work - advancing our commitment to locally led action and building strong, values-driven relationships with network members and other strategic partners. This role will lead and be accountable for the development and delivery of the HelpAge network strategy, ensuring alignment with our global mission and enabling inclusive, sustainable collaboration across the HelpAge network. The postholder provides strategic leadership for network engagement, development and capacity strengthening across all regions - Africa, Asia, Eurasia and the Middle East, Europe, and Latin America and the Caribbean. They lead through the Regional Advisers rather than delivering regional workstreams personally: setting annual priorities and deliverables for each region, in alignment with organisational priorities, and hold Regional Advisers accountable for delivery through regular performance management and review. This is an evolving role. The postholder ensures the capacity strengthening and localisation offer is shaped by what members themselves identify as their needs and differentiated by region and member segment, rather than applied uniformly. They lead the mechanisms that connect global and regional levels of the network - regional convenings, member-to-member exchange, and the flow of regional intelligence into global strategy, positioning and funding decisions. The role works in close partnership with internal stakeholders - Executive Leadership Group, Board, Leadership Group, and Team Heads - and external stakeholders including network members, civil society organisations, local consortia, donors, and institutional partners. The postholder leads the preparation and quality of Governance Committee submissions and Board papers on network development and engagement. Alongside this regional remit, the role holder will lead directly on coordinating members in the Europe region, and work closely with the Head of Advocacy and Evidencing to develop our strategic niche on donor advocacy in Europe. Key areas for impact/influence and responsibilities To make an impact and influence, the role holder will shape and deliver the HelpAge network strategy and HelpAge's transition to locally led ways of working; provide strategic oversight of network member engagement, localisation, and the organisational capacity sharing strategy; lead HelpAge's support to country transitions, including Ukraine; and build an inclusive, resilient and effective global network of local and national organisations. Network strategy and impact Lead delivery of the HelpAge network strategy, ensuring it supports locally led transitions, strong partnerships and member engagement. Lead the Thriving Network Impact Vehicle (one of six priority areas through which HelpAge delivers its strategy; the other five target external policy change - social pensions, health coverage, humanitarian action, legal rights, climate adaptation - while this one targets the health and sustainability of the network itself) and its results framework, ensuring a clear connection between day-to-day activities and HelpAge's 2030 network targets, and reporting quarterly to the senior leadership team on progress. Lead the preparation and quality assurance of Governance Committee submissions (membership applications, ambassador appointments) and Board papers relating to network development and engagement. Regional leadership Line manage the Regional Advisers. Set annual regional priorities and delivery accountabilities aligned to the network and advocacy strategies, and hold each Regional Adviser accountable for delivery through regular performance management and review. Hold direct responsibility for engagement with Europe-based members, and work with the Head of Advocacy and Evidencing to develop HelpAge's strategic niche on donor advocacy in Europe. Set the strategic frame for network convenings - purpose, frequency, participant profile and hold Regional Advisers accountable for regional and thematic convenings. Chair the strategic reference group INDABA, HelpAge's consultative forum with network members. Membership and capacity sharing Lead and oversee the network membership lifecycle - recruitment, accreditation, due diligence, segmentation and exit - using segmentation to determine how each member is engaged and what level of capacity sharing support they receive, in line with HelpAge's governance frameworks and agreed decision-making authorities. Lead delivery of the Network Capacity Sharing Strategy, translating it into a coherent network-wide offer, integrated across programmes, in collaboration with Programme Support, Advocacy and Evidencing and other relevant teams. Hold the Humanitarian Capacity Strengthening Manager accountable for delivery in priority humanitarian contexts and the SCORE Programme Manager for delivery against SCORE commitments, with both required to feed learning back into the offer; facilitate alignment across different programme approaches and escalate cross-functional issues where appropriate.. Hold the Network Platform Manager 1 accountable for member collaboration platforms that support the network strategy, capacity sharing and member onboarding. Localisation and country transitions Line manage the Network Support Lead. Set the strategic framework for localisation and country transition support and hold them accountable for delivery across relevant country transitions. Ensure network and localisation commitments are reflected in country strategies, programme design and partner engagement, working in collaboration with the Advocacy and Evidencing and Programme Support teams. Resources, Risk Management and Representation Be accountable for achieving the agreed Network Development income target. Working in partnership with the Fundraising & Strategic Partnerships (F&SP) team, play a lead technical and relationship role in shaping fundable propositions, contributing to pipeline development, including ownership of priority donor relationships and the funding pipeline**,** donor cultivation and stewardship, and fundraising for network convening, capacity sharing and the knowledge platform. Act as budget holder for the Network Development portfolio, including grant budgets, with accountability for forecasting, spend against budget, cost recovery and donor compliance. Ensure that organisational standards, policies and frameworks relating to safeguarding, security, fraud and other relevant risks are effectively embedded across Network Development activities, working with the relevant functional leads and holding team leads accountable for compliance within their areas and programmes. Represent HelpAge in global fora on localisation and partnerships, positioning HelpAge as a credible voice on localisation, locally led development, civil society networks, and the role of older people and their organisations - contributing to thought leadership and sector-wide learning. Skills and experience required Essential Proven strategic leadership of a membership network, alliance or partnership portfolio in the international development, humanitarian or civil society sectors, including responsibility for network strategy and its delivery. Demonstrated ability to lead through senior managers - setting the strategic frame, agreeing accountabilities and holding others to delivery - rather than personally owning workstreams. Experience managing diverse, multi-disciplinary and geographically dispersed teams. Extensive experience working with and supporting civil society networks, grassroots organisations and local partners, particularly in low- and middle-income or Global South contexts. Strong knowledge of and commitment to Partner-Led Programming principles, with a proven record of advancing localisation and supporting organisational transitions to locally led ways of working. Experience of the membership lifecycle in a network or alliance - recruitment, accreditation, due diligence and, where necessary, exit. And of segmentation to inform how members are engaged and supported. Track record of income generation against a target, including named ownership of institutional donor relationships and management of a funding pipeline. Budget-holding experience at portfolio level, including grant budgets, forecasting, cost recovery and donor compliance. Experience leading the implementation of a results framework and reporting on progress against strategic targets to an executive or board-level audience. Strong understanding of safeguarding, equity and inclusion, and a demonstrated ability to embed these across teams and partnerships and to hold others accountable for doing so. Excellent communication and interpersonal skills, with the ability to build trusted relationships with network members, donors, civil society organisations and institutional actors, and to navigate disagreement between them. Lived experience of the Global South or significant professional experience working in Global South contexts. Desirable Experience designing and delivering a differentiated capacity sharing or capacity strengthening offer across a diverse membership, informed by member-identified need rather than a single global package. Experience of governance processes in a membership body - preparing submissions for a governance committee or board on membership, accreditation or appointments. Experience convening members at regional or global level, including designing convenings for genuine exchange rather than presentation. Familiarity with ageing, inclusion and rights issues in Global South contextsEducation and Qualification Education and Qualifications Degree in international development, public policy, human rights, social sciences, or a related field (or equivalent professional experience). A postgraduate qualification is an asset but not essential where practical experience is strong. Values, Skills, and Ways of Working Ability to work across cultures, sectors, and geographies in inclusive and equitable ways. Excellent communication skills in English (spoken and written); additional languages used in the Global South (e.g., Spanish, French, Arabic) are highly desirable. Deep commitment to locally led development and the principles of Partner-Led Programming. We actively value and encourage candidates with lived experience of inequality, marginalisation, or systemic exclusion—especially related to age, gender, disability, displacement, or economic injustice. Key Behavioural Competencies Working Collaboratively with Others Work collaboratively, building mutual trust and respect, with external organizations and partners to achieve our strategic aims and objectives; being accountable for the work we do together. Adaptability and Flexibility Adapt to new directions or opportunities arising within the organisation and in our work area; being flexible in our role, constantly using the feedback to learn more and evolve further. Supporting and Facilitating Change Lead behavioural and cultural change through embracing a supportive, collaborative and highly inclusive environment where everybody feels supported, respected and engaged. Extend HelpAge’s Reach and Impact Extend HelpAge’s reach and impact by creating and identifying new business development opportunities andbuilding relationships withnew partners. Diversity and Inclusion Lead and promote a culture of including the voices of older people across our support, convening and thoughtleadership roles, in a way that is transformative, empowering and highly inclusive of those marginalised by gender, economic status, disability and other factors of discrimination. Leading Others (for managers) Demonstrate strong leadership to own unit/department and manage people in a well and reputable manner. Create an atmosphere of trust and an enabling environment where staff can contribute their best and develop their potential. Safeguarding HelpAge International is committed to safeguarding the communities with which we work, our partners, staff and any others who we come into contact with. The post holder will also be responsible for: Preventing harm and abuse from our people, operations and programmes to anyone that encounters our work. Reporting all safeguarding incidents you see, hear, hear about or suspect, using our internal reporting mechanism. Complying with all safeguarding framework policies and practices. Completing mandatory training courses relating to our safeguarding policy framework and complying with HR vetting procedures. SAFER RECRUITMENT All employments at HelpAge International will be subject to satisfactory references and appropriate screening checks, which can include misconduct disclosure schemes and terrorism finance checks.

How to Apply: All qualified and experienced candidates are encouraged to review the full job description and submit a cover letter and CV to **jobs@helpage.org by 5 October 2026**. Applicants must have the right to work and live in the identified location.

title: Senior Portfolio Manager, Inclusive Health
description:
About CBM CBM (registered as CBM Christoffel-Blindenmission Christian Blind Mission e.V.) is an international development organisation committed to improving the quality of life of persons with disabilities in the persons communities of the world. Based on our Christian values and more than 100 years of professional expertise, we address poverty as a cause and a consequence of disability. We work in partnership to create an inclusive society for all. About the role: The Senior Portfolio Manager leads the development of innovative programmes within the Inclusive Health Initiative (IHI), designing project portfolios that support broader country programme goals. The role strengthens coordination across sectoral activities, fosters strong partnerships with national counterparts, and advances CBM's mission through high-quality programme leadership. This position will be filled locally in one of CBM's permanent established entities (e.g. Bensheim (Germany), Cambridge (UK), Nairobi (Kenya), Abuja (Nigeria), Lomé (Togo), Yaoundé (Cameroon), Lusaka (Zambia), Addis Ababa (Ethiopia), Kampala (Uganda), Niamey (Niger), etc.). This position is only filled locally. With contractual conditions of the respective country. An expatriation is not intended. You Will: Set the multi-year strategic direction for the IHI portfolio, including resource allocation, risk management, and innovation priorities across Eye Health, Ear & Hearing Health, and Physical Rehabilitation. Provide strategic oversight of participatory project design processes in assigned countries, including the development of logical frameworks, budgets, and implementation plans. Ensure high-quality programme delivery, robust monitoring, and effective evaluation processes. Ensure the IHI strategy is reflected in the development of CBM country plans and aligned with the Inclusive Health Initiative Strategy. Directly line-manage, mentor, and performance-review IHI Portfolio Managers, providing strategic guidance and setting priorities. Lead proposal development, including programme design, budgeting, and donor negotiations, working closely with IHI Portfolio Managers to incorporate country-level programme inputs. Oversee initiative-level programme monitoring, including cross-country synthesis and strategic reviews. Track programme outputs across the Initiative and ensure corrective actions are implemented across all IHI countries. Develop programme and Board-level reports and leadership briefings. Coordinate IHI partner engagement and represent the Initiative in key programme and sector forums. Promote cross-sector collaboration and integrated approaches to inclusive health programming. Champion safeguarding, disability inclusion, and high standards of programme quality. These are your qualifications A Master's degree in Public Health, Rehabilitation Sciences, Social Sciences, Development Studies, or a related field. At least 10 years' experience managing complex health or development programmes. Experience across multiple health areas; experience with digital health tools or health information systems is an advantage. Experience in directly line-managing programme teams. A proven track record in donor engagement and proposal development. Experience representing organisations in global and policy forums, including with the UN, governments, and donor roundtables. Knowledge of policy frameworks, sector standards, and practices in at least one of the three IHI health areas. Proven experience in project cycle management, monitoring and evaluation (M&E), and budgeting. Strong partnership management, coordination, team leadership, communication, problem-solving, and organisational skills. Ability to work independently and collaboratively in multicultural settings. Excellent English language skills; knowledge of French or Spanish is an added advantage. A demonstrated commitment to disability inclusion and safeguarding principles. Identification with the mission, values, and mandate of CBM What we offer A meaningful position with a lot of creative freedom in the world's leading organisation in the field of Disability Inclusive Development A fair salary and other social benefits based on the local conditions in the country you apply for An approachable, agile organisation with self-reliant people in a diverse and collegial team and great team spirit

How to Apply: ### **How to apply** Please apply exclusively online via our applicant portal (see [APPLY NOW](https://jobs.cbm.org/Senior-Portfolio-Manager-Inclusive-Health-eng-f1086.html)). A letter of motivation, CV and relevant (work) references complete your application. We look forward to receiving your application! Your contact person: Ms. Eve Muthama We would like to further promote diversity in our teams and therefore welcome applications from people of different ethnic and social backgrounds, religions and world views, different ages and genders, and especially from people with disabilities. Suitability is decisive, gender is irrelevant!

title: Country Representative for Ethiopia, Based in Addis Ababa
description:
WHAT IS IMPACT INITIATIVES ? OUR AIM: IMPACT aims to shape practices and influence policies in humanitarian and development settings, in order to positively impact the lives of people and their communities. Created in 2010, IMPACT is a Geneva-based NGO and the largest independent data provider in contexts of crisis. We aim to support a range of stakeholders in making better, more informed decisions in humanitarian, stabilisation, and development settings. We believe that a key pathway to better planning and decision-making is direct engagement with local communities. HOW DO WE WORK ? IMPACT takes an initiative-based approach to structuring our programming. Each initiative has a specific aim, operational model, and portfolio of solutions. REACH strengthens evidence-based humanitarian decision-making through efficient data collection, management, and analysis - before, during, and after an emergency. PANDA improves the impact of humanitarian and development interventions through programme design, assessments, and monitoring & evaluation. AGORA promotes localised and multi-sectoral aid action in support of the recovery and stabilisation of crisis-affected communities, in partnership with local stakeholders Through our global team of research specialists, on average IMPACT publishes more than 1,700 information products on a yearly basis. In 2010, IMPACT was launched at the initiative of ACTED, an international NGO whose headquarters are based in Paris and is present in thirty countries. The two organizations have a strong complementarity formalized in a global partnership, which particularly allows IMPACT to benefit from ACTED’s operational support in its fields of intervention. We are currently looking for a Country Representative to lead our Ethiopia mission, based in Addis Abeba Position: Country Representative Contract duration: 12 months Location: Addis Abeba, Ethiopia, with potential travel to Kampala, Uganda Starting Date: October / November 2026 Application Deadline: 09 October 2026. COUNTRY PROFILE Since 2018, Ethiopia has experienced escalating insecurity and unrest, including large-scale displacement, loss of life, and widespread destruction of property, following significant domestic political changes. These crises have compounded the effects of recurring climate-related shocks affecting large parts of the country. In November 2020, conflict erupted in the northern Tigray region, triggering significant displacement across Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions. Since August 2023, renewed conflict in Amhara has further intensified humanitarian needs, leading to the declaration of a state of emergency and restrictions on movement across the region. Together, these crises have severely disrupted livelihoods, constrained access to essential goods and staple commodities, and increased the vulnerability of affected populations, placing additional pressure on humanitarian response capacities across the country. FUNCTIONS Under the management of IMPACT’s Regional Coordinator (RC) for Africa in Geneva, the Country Representative (CR) is responsible for representing IMPACT and managing and developing IMPACT’s programmes in Ethiopia. S/he leads the IMPACT team to achieve program excellence and ensure the highest level of impact and accountability, while ensuring compliance to IMPACT guidelines, policies and standards across the mission. The CR is in regular contact with HQ, ensuring that organizational risks are promptly and clearly communicated to the Regional Coordinator and other relevant HQ Senior Management. S/he will promote organizational vision and core values across the mission and will actively link with HQ to contribute to the implementation of IMPACT’s global strategy. In his/her mission, the Country Representative will be hosted by Acted and will fall under the direct responsibility and management of Acted’s Country Director for all Administrative, Security, Logistics and Finance issues. S/he will therefore fully abide by Acted’s Security, HR, Administration and Logistics rules and regulations, and, in coordination with Acted, will ensure that all IMPACT staff abide by them. RESPONSIBILITIES The Country Representative responsibilities include the following: Strategic Leadership Develop and execute an up-to-date Country Strategy aligned with IMPACT’s global objectives and Ethiopia’s humanitarian landscape. Identify strategic opportunities, consolidate ongoing initiatives, and explore new programme areas to enhance IMPACT’s value to the aid community. Programme and Project Management In coordination with the Deputy Country Representative, oversee programme planning, implementation, and evaluation, ensuring all projects meet objectives, timelines, and compliance standards. Facilitate coordination between IMPACT and partner organizations to achieve efficient project delivery and impact. Fundraising and Donor Engagement Identify and secure funding opportunities in collaboration with HQ and Acted. Lead proposal development and negotiate contracts with donors, ensuring alignment with strategic priorities. Operations Support the Operations Managers and Project Development and Partnership Officers in building and maintaining a broad network of partner organizations to strengthen operational capacity and facilitate the implementation of activities in hard-to-reach and underserved areas. Continue to explore alternative operational models and innovative research approaches to expand geographic and population coverage, particularly among marginalized and difficult-to-reach communities. Ensure regular coordination with Acted's project development and FLATS departments (finance, logistics, administration, transparency, security) at all stages of project development and implementation. Finance and Budget Oversight Manage project budgets and forecast expenses, ensuring accurate and timely financial reporting to HQ and Acted. Mitigate financial risks and ensure optimal budget utilization. Human Resources and Team Leadership In consultation with the Deputy Country Representative, guide and develop the IMPACT team, ensuring performance standards, capacity building, and adherence to IMPACT and Acted’s policies. Coordinate with HQ and Acted for transparent recruitment and career management of staff. External Representation and Coordination Establish and maintain productive relationships with donors, UN agencies, NGOs, and other stakeholders, representing IMPACT’s programmes and strategic interests. Ensure proactive contribution to key humanitarian decision-making forums and promote IMPACT’s programme visibility. Data Protection and Accountability Uphold strict confidentiality of all data collected and engage with communities respectfully, ensuring awareness of programme objectives and methods. REQUIREMENTS Academic qualifications: Excellent academic qualifications, including a Master’s degree in a relevant discipline (International Relations, Political Sciences, Social Research, Development Studies, or similar). Management experience: Previous experience in a senior management role in an INGO at field level. Track record in successful management of international and national teams in humanitarian contexts. Familiarity with aid system: Familiarity with the aid system, and the research community. Communication/reporting skills: Excellent communication and drafting skills for effective reporting, including proven experience in contributing to high level presentations/briefings. Years of work experience: At least 5 years of relevant working experience. Any previous experience in Ethiopia would be an asset. Research skills: Experience in assessments. M&E, field research, evaluations an asset. Multi-tasking skills: Ability to multitask with tight deadlines in complex environment. Level of independence: A self-starter with a proven ability to work independently. Cross-cultural work environment: Ability to operate in a cross-cultural environment. Language skills: Fluency in English required**.** Security environment: Ability to operate in a complex and challenging security environment. COMPENSATION AND BENEFITS For this position, salary between 4’050€ and 4’100€ monthly (before income tax), etc as well as a monthly living allowance of 500 USD NB - IMPACT salaries are strictly determined by our salary grid depending on the grade of the position and the level of education of staff. A location-dependent security and/or isolation adjustment is then applied as a recognition that some staff are required to work in hardship places where living and working conditions are much more difficult than elsewhere. Accommodation and food provided in ACTED guesthouse Private pension fund, health insurance, and repatriation assistance (& unemployment insurance for EU citizens) This is not a family duty station Flight tickets every 6 months & visa fees covered Contribution to the luggage transportation: between 23kg and 100kg, depending on the length of the contract Annual leave of 36 days per year Predeparture induction - 3 days at IMPACT Initiatives’s HQ in Geneva + one week pre-departure training in ACTED HQ in Paris, including a 4-days in situ security training Tax advice (free 30-minute call with a tax consultant) Enrolment in IMPACT Initiatives Research Foundational Learning Programme within the first 3 months from the start of contract. IMPACT and ACTED prioritize the psychological safety of its staff and the health insurance provided covers, among others, up to 1000 € per year of psychosocial counselling fees.

How to Apply: Please apply directly on the website via the following link: [Country Representative for Ethiopia, Based in Addis Ababa (Link For External Applicants) | Impact](https://www.impact-initiatives.org/work-with-us/vacancies/country-representative-for-ethiopia-based-in-addis-ababa-link-for-external-applicants/)

title: Africa Resource Mobilisation and Partnerships Manager
description:
Location: Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania or Zimbabwe, with a preference for Ethiopia/East Africa *Kenya is subject to HelpAge International maintaining its registration in the country. Department: Network Development Team, Global Impact Directorate Reports to (Line Manager): Regional Adviser, Africa Responsible for( Line managing): N/A Grade: Grade D Contract Type: Fixed-term 12 months, with scope to extend subject to funding About HelpAge HelpAge International works with a diverse global network of around 200 organisations across 99 countries to promote the rights of older people to lead dignified, healthy and secure lives. Through partnership and collaborations, we work to ensure the inclusion of older people across society and strive to deliver a just and fair world for everyone as they get older. Our work is driven by our desire to achieve real impact for older people, to be inclusive, to work in partnership and to learn from our shared experience. About the Job The Africa Ageing Conference is being developed as a flagship biennial continental platform to advance leadership, collaboration, learning, accountability and investment on ageing, longevity and demographic change. It will bring together older people, network members, governments, regional institutions, civil society, academia, development partners, philanthropies and the private sector around a shared agenda for ageing-inclusive development. The postholder will lead the day-to-day opportunity development, donor cultivation and partnership engagement for the Africa Ageing Conference, developing the funding pipeline, investment case, donor cultivation strategy and external partnerships required to support both successful delivery and longer-term impact. It will also contribute to wider resource mobilisation and partnership priorities emerging from the Africa Plan and Africa Coordination Mechanism. All of this work will be undertaken within HelpAge's agreed fundraising, due diligence and approval processes. While the line manager is the Regional Adviser for Africa, the Fundraising & Strategic Partnerships Team will provide organisational oversight and support on donor relationship management, proposal development, negotiation and contracting, with all formal commitments subject to appropriate organisational approval. Key areas for impact/influence and responsibilities 1. Resource Mobilisation and Funding Development Lead the development and implementation of the Africa Ageing Conference resource mobilisation and partnership plan, under the strategic direction of the Regional Adviser, Africa and aligned with organisational fundraising priorities and agreed targets. Develop and maintain a prioritised pipeline of funding, sponsorship and in-kind opportunities for the Conference, with clear ownership of opportunities, status, next steps and assessment of strategic fit. Develop compelling investment propositions, concept notes, proposals, sponsorship packages and pitch materials in collaboration with the Conference team, Regional Advisor, Africa, Fundraising & Strategic Partnerships Team and relevant technical, finance and communications colleagues. Progress opportunities from research and cultivation through to proposal and stewardship, ensuring agreements are concluded through relevant organisational approval processes. 2. Strategic Partnerships and External Engagement Identify, cultivate and maintain relationships with prospective funders, sponsors, network members and strategic partners relevant to the Conference and agreed Africa priorities. Represent HelpAge in approved external engagements, present funding propositions and explore partner interests within agreed parameters, escalating proposed terms or commitments for internal review and approval. Identify partnership opportunities aligned with the Conference, Africa Plan and organisational priorities, and advise colleagues on strategic fit, risks and routes to engagement. 3. Africa Ageing Conference Lead the day-to-day resource mobilisation and partnership workstream for the Africa Ageing Conference, ensuring fundraising activity responds to agreed Conference plans, programme priorities and resource requirements. Work closely with the Africa Conference and Regional Platform Coordinator and Conference Planning and Coordination Team to coordinate the internal and external inputs required to progress funding and partnership opportunities. Support the stewardship of Conference funders, sponsors and partners before, during and after the event, and identify longer-term opportunities connected to Conference outcomes and legacy. 4. Coordination and Internal Collaboration Work closely with the Regional Adviser, Africa, Head of Network Development and Fundraising & Strategic Partnerships Team to align activity with organisational priorities, donor ownership arrangements and fundraising processes. Coordinate technical, financial, communications, due diligence, risk and approval inputs, recognising that specialist teams and authorised decision-makers retain accountability for approval and sign-off. Maintain accurate records and provide regular reporting on the funding and partnership pipeline, progress against agreed objectives, risks, decisions and next steps. 5. Wider Africa Resource Mobilisation Contribute to resource mobilisation and partnership development for agreed priorities emerging from the Africa Plan and Africa Coordination Mechanism, within priorities established by the Regional Adviser, Africa and relevant organisational teams. Use relationships and intelligence generated through the Conference to identify relevant wider opportunities, including collaborative approaches with network members and regional partners. Identify and assess emerging funding and partnership opportunities and make recommendations on their strategic fit and potential for progression. Skills and experience required Essential Degree in international development, fundraising, business development, public policy, international relations, social sciences or a related field, or equivalent professional experience. Substantial experience in fundraising, strategic partnerships, business development, sponsorship or donor engagement in an international or regional context. Demonstrable experience developing and managing funding or sponsorship pipelines and progressing prospects from research and cultivation through to proposals and stewardship. Experience developing support for major conferences, events, platforms, campaigns or multi-stakeholder initiatives. Strong prospect research and analysis skills, including assessment of strategic fit, eligibility, risks and routes to engagement. Experience producing compelling investment propositions, concept notes, proposals, sponsorship packages, pitch materials and partner-facing communications. Demonstrable experience and confidence independently engaging prospective funders, sponsors and senior external stakeholders, including leading face-to-face and virtual meetings and presenting funding propositions. Experience working with civil society networks, membership organisations, regional platforms or multi-partner coalitions. Excellent written communication, coordination and information-management skills, with strong attention to detail. Ability to manage multiple relationships, opportunities and deadlines across countries, cultures and time zones. Fluency in English. Desirable Knowledge of African Union, Regional Economic Community or United Nations coordination structures. Experience securing support from institutional donors, foundations, trusts, corporate partners or philanthropies in Africa. About One Acre Fund Founded in 2006, One Acre Fund equips 5.5 million smallholder farmers to make their farms more productive. Across nine countries that together are home to two-thirds of Africa's farmers, we provide high-quality farm supplies, tree seedlings, accessible credit, modern agronomic training, and a wide range of other agricultural services. On average, this model enables any farmer to increase their income and assets on supported land by more than 35 percent, while permanently improving their resilience. This is all made possible by our team of 9,000+ full-time staff, drawn from diverse backgrounds and professions. To learn more, please see our Why Work Here blog post. In Ethiopia, we engage farmers in agroforestry and community-based seed multiplication to increase farmers’ incomes and make farming systems more resilient. Engaging with local actors at every step but bringing innovative ideas from outside, we are making rural farming more market-friendly and environmentally sustainable. The farmers we work with in Ethiopia have planted more than 30 million trees, produced over 1500 metric tonnes of improved teff seed, and improved the futures of nearly 200,000 community members. Our permanent team numbers over 180 with nearly 1,000 rural seasonal staff supporting them. Our country headquarters are in Addis Ababa and we have a large program office in Bahir Dar, plus several smaller field offices. title: Consultant - Final Evaluation Coherence programme Ethiopia
description:
1. Introduction The COHERENCE programme Ethiopia 2022-2026 is implemented by Ethiopian Catholic Church – Social and Development Commission Soddo branch (ECC-SDCO/S) and Adigrat branch (ECC-SDCO/Ad) , with coordination support by the East Africa regional programme Manager CI.be. The programme is implemented in 7 countries and is co-funded by the Belgian Government. The program’s aim is to equip rural communities so that they become more resilient and can better cope with crisis situations. Above all, the program wants the most vulnerable people, particularly women, young people and people with disabilities, to have expanded opportunities to improve their living conditions. Through a ‘triple nexus ’ approach, focus is on (1) social cohesion, peace-building and rights protection within communities; (2) rural economic development; and (3) disaster preparedness The present terms of reference relate exclusively to the final evaluation of COHERENCE Ethiopia. The final evaluations of the three other country programs are the subject of separate tenders and fall outside the scope of this assignment. 2. Object of the evaluation: COHERENCE Ethiopia 2.1 Program objective, results and activities To address food insecurity of poor and vulnerable households – with a focus on female-headed and landless households – of 2 kebeles in Damot Woyde district (Wolaita) and 2 kebeles in Irob district (Eastern Tigray) , COHERENCE Ethiopia aimed to improve their livelihood base in a sustainable way, by means of a triple nexus approach, linking three complementary areas: social cohesion, rural economic development and disaster risk reduction (DRR). The action’s specific objective was formulated as follows: “By the end of 2026, poor and vulnerable households, especially resource poor female-headed and landless households, in two kebeles (Endamosa and Hareze Sabata) of Irob district and two kebeles (Kindo Koyo and Mayo Kote) of Damot Woyde district have strengthened their livelihood basis, better enabling them to seize opportunities and realize their aspirations”. The objective was to be achieved through three results. A first result concerned social cohesion that was to be improved by building household and community capacity to manage resource-induced conflicts and to ensure equitable and fair access or entitlement to natural resources, through, among others: Conducting a rapid gender context analysis at community level (1 in each intervention area); Organizing in groups and training of 180 community cohesion and gender empowerment agents on peace building, conflict management and facilitation skills; Organizing community dialogue sessions on peace and conflict management and gender equity (while applying the household transformation method); Rehabilitating and expanding water piping to address existing water access conflict (Wolaita); Planting tree seedlings on communal land between communities as a joint, social cohesion enhancing activity (Tigray); Providing energy-saving stoves for 300 households (Wolaita). The direct causes of food insecurity in the intervention zones are – besides the two-year war in Tigray (2020-2022) – the depletion of household assets and continuous dwindling of income. Repeated food shortages have also forced many households to sell their assets to address immediate needs. Therefore, through a second result , the program aimed to contribute to improving household production, income, savings and productive assets by: Supporting households in income generating activities and household asset building; Organizing, training and equipping savings and and internal lending groups (SILCs) to enhance solidarity, savings and resilience; Selecting specific Household Asset Building Packages (HABP), providing technical and basic business training of HABP-SILC groups, and supporting households in financing business plans by means of subsidy. Finally, a third result sought to strengthen vulnerable households' resilience in response to climate-induced shocks and stress, by focusing on improving farm production by: Organizing volunteer smallholders in “community learning groups” (type of farmer field schools) and providing orientation training on Resilience Design (RD); Facilitating self-assessments based on local knowledge, practices and exchange; Increasing soil fertility with appropriate durable techniques identified using a RD approach; Supplying farm-resilient seeds and biological catalysator (for compost making) (Tigray); Providing energy-saving tools for households with special needs; Conducting quality monitoring and group learning of RD-related activities implemented at farm-level through community learning groups or famer field school groups. In addition, by means of workshops, exchange visits, networking and inclusive and participatory MEAL, stakeholders were expected to mutually reinforce each other's capacities, in particular with regard to issues addressed by the program. 2.2 Target groups COHERENCE Ethiopia’s implementation period extended over 42 and 36 months respectively in Wolaita and Eastern Tigray, addressing a total of at least 1,900 households (1,000 in Wolaita and 900 in Eastern Tigray). More specifically, the program targeted: With regard to social cohesion: 1,900 households (1,000 in Wolaita, 900 in Tigray) of which 1,327 are male-headed (787 in Wolaita, 540 in Tigray) and 573 female-headed (213 in Wolaita, 360 in Tigray), 4 peace and social cohesion and gender equity promoting groups, and 180 peace and social cohesion agents / community leaders (elders, religious leaders, women and youth representatives, …) (75 in Wolaita, 105 in Tigray); With regard to rural economic development (household asset building): 830 poor households (400 in Wolaita, 430 in Tigray) with priority for female-headed and landless households, and 49 SILCs (20 in Wolaita, 29 in Tigray); With regard to disaster risk reduction (resilience design): 800 smallholder households (600 in Wolaita, 200 in Tigray), with a priority for smallholders vulnerable to climate change; Government technical staff. In addition to these target-groups, i.e. direct beneficiaries, the following indirect beneficiaries were foreseen: The population of the 2 kebeles (Endamosa and Hareze Sabata) in Eastern Tigray and of the 2 kebeles (Kindo Koyo and Mayo Kote) in Wolaita; Government services and local authorities of the 4 kebeles; Authorities of Irob and Damot Woyde districts. 2.3 Three innovative approaches Three approaches are assumed to have particularly contributed to the action’s achievements and are to receive specific attention during the final evaluation (see evaluation questions below). 2.3.1 Social cohesion and peace building through village peace agents To encourage peace building and social cohesion, COHERENCE Ethiopia mobilized volunteers from the targeted communities who were expected to become “change agents”.They were trained on basic peace building and conflict management and thus equipped with knowledge and skills on grassroots conflict prevention, management and resolution. Thereto, the program adopted the so-called the 3Bs/4Ds methodology (cf. https://ics.crs.org/resource/ties-bind-building-social-cohesion-divided-communities ) that combines binding, bonding and bridging (the 3Bs) with appreciative inquiry (the 4Ds: discover, dream, design and deliver) to enable communities to cooperate and collaborate across ethnic, religious, gender, class and other divides and to strengthen horizontal and vertical rights relations and social cohesion. Following this methodology, key grassroots actors were accompanied in discovering their individual and collective strengths and their mutual responsibilities in promoting social cohesion. At the heart of the methodology is a focus on what connects and energizes people, rather than on obstacles and issues that separate them. The trained change agents were to facilitate “community dialogues sessions” that focused on tensions and conflicts that had been identified through a rapid conflict analysis and a limited social cohesion barometer survey. 2.3.2 Gender empowerment Apart from promoting peace and social cohesion, the community volunteers were also expected to be change agents with regard to gender relations in their community. They were trained on gender analysis and participatory gender transformative methods and tools. A rapid gender context analysis was conducted and based on its findings, gender transformation activities were engaged in by the program at two levels. First, at village level, trained change agents organized, in collaboration with the program’s community animators, community conversation sessions on gender issues with groups of men and women, giving participants room to talk, discuss and exchange ideas about gender perceptions and roles in their households and at community level. Next, using two complementary gender transformation methods (the Household Transformation Method (HTM) and Gender Action Learning (GAL) ), male and female members of households were supported in assessing and analyzing intra-household gender disparities (division of labor, access to and control of household resources, benefits sharing mechanisms, decision-making power, etc.). Ultimately, the approach was to result in bringing about change and improvement in terms of the gender empowerment index. 2.3.3 Community Learning Groups Co-creation and sharing of knowledge plays a central role in the process of developing and implementing agroecological innovations including climate change adaptation. To create together and share knowledge, farmers need a platform that supports them to work in small groups and have opportunities to articulate ideas, increase their motivation and participation to innovate and adapt, build trust and collaborate among themselves and with other stakeholders (e.g. extension workers) and strengthen effective linkages with stakeholders. One way in which co-creation and knowledge sharing can be encouraged is by establishing and strengthening Community Learning Groups (CLG) at grassroots. While in other approaches Farmer Field Schools (FFS) or Farmer Training Centers (FTC) are used as centers where people go and learn or acquire knowledge, a CLG is a group of active and interested individual farmers organized for peer-to-peer learning and experience or knowledge sharing, regardless of age, sex and social group. Most of the time, experience sharing and visiting events take place among members and external experts and trainers are invited on demand only. Farmers participating in the Ethiopia program thus established such CLGs. While participating in these groups, they implemented resilience design activities concerning soil health, soil and water conservation and crop diversification. Group membership is based on proximity of farmland. The program strengthened the CLGs’ capacity by means of an orientation session and training on the CLG approach and its objectives and its added value compared with other extension approaches. With the support of the program, the CLGs established bylaws and appointed their leadership (chairperson, secretary and record keeper). They meet once per month to share experiences and to learn. For each meeting the agenda – including issues for discussion, whether or not to invite external persons, etc. – is set by the CLG leaders in consultation with members. The CLG members visit each other’s farm, possibly accompanied by a development agent (DA), to see and exchange on and learn from the resilience design activities that were accomplished at the farm. The CLG approach was expected to encourage dissemination of good practices within and outside communities. Within a community, larger CLGs could be divided into smaller ones at village-level or below, so that the number of people participating in experience exchange could be multiplied. The budget of COHERENCE Ethiopia is 849,799 Euro. 3. Purpose and objectives of the evaluation The final evaluation of the COHERENCE Ethiopia program aims at: Identifying lessons learned in the introduction and adoption of social methodological innovation in view of future programming by CI.be and its partners; Ensuring accountability towards donors and other stakeholders , by rendering public the results of program performance assessment. These two objectives will be accomplished by answering three evaluation questions concerning the implementation of the three methodological approaches – presented above in § 2.3. – within the overall HDP nexus perspective. These approaches – respectively involving village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups – are considered innovative and key to the achievement of the program’s outcome. The intended users of the final evaluation’s results include the following: Implementation and coordination teams of partners ECC-SDCO/Ad and ECC-SDCO/S; CI.be staff at regional offices and head office and partner staff involved in joint development programming; Staff of other development actors (through publication of the final evaluation report on the CI.be website); DGD, the program donor (accountability). 4. Scope of the evaluation, evaluation criteria and evaluation questions With regard to its scope, the final evaluation will cover the COHERENCE Ethiopia program in both intervention areas, that is, in both Wolaita and Eastern Tigray, although – given the uncertain security situation in Tigray – fieldwork is expected to be restricted to solely Wolaita. Focus will be on the performance of three innovative methodological approaches, implemented by the program within a nexus approach: village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups. The DAC criteria that will be taken into account include coherence , effectiveness and sustainability . In addition, particular attention will be paid to the performance of the intervention in terms of inclusiveness in the fight against poverty and organisational strengthening of the target groups. The following evaluation questions are proposed (to be refined and prioritised during the framing phase): To what extent was the nexus approach adopted by the program appropriate and adequate foraddressing the target groups’ priority needs? [DAC criteria: coherence and sustainability] To what extent were the pathways of change and assumptions (theory of change) and the intervention logic (results framework) coherent, plausible and feasible? To what extent were the three innovative approaches (village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups) critical in the adopted design of the nexus approach? To what extent did they contribute to integrating the three pillars of the nexus (synergies between the pillars)? To what extent did the innovations fall short in reaching the different vulnerable groups targeted by the program (LNOB)? What have been the roles and contributions of the three innovative approaches (village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups) in achieving program outcomes ? [DAC criteria: effectiveness and sustainability] To what extent and how have the three innovative approaches beeneffective in bringing about behavioral change and adoption of new practices at target group level? Which are the factors that were conducive to these changes ? Which factors can be identified that have hindered or slowed down changes? To what extent did the 3 methods function better than other existing alternative methods in achieving program outcomes? To what extent and how are the three innovative approaches transformative? Can we see early signs of enduring changes in norms and systems ? To what extent has the program created enabling mechanisms to sustain the positive effects induced by the three innovative approaches?[DAC criteria: coherence and sustainability] How appropriate was the process of introducing the three innovative approaches within the targeted communities? Did the program learn from and adapt these innovative approaches or other activities during their implementation? What was the contribution of the MEAL process in this? To what extent do the stakeholders of the intervention – including government actiors and target groups – take ownership of the results achieved by means of the three innovative approaches and how committed are they to sustaining these results after the program’s closure? To what extent has the program built capacities of key stakeholders (implementing partners, government sector offices and target groups) required to institutionalize the innovative approaches without forsaking grassroots ownership and leadership and allowing continued flow of benefits? For each evaluation question clear and relevant lessons on introducing innovations are to be identified for use in the formulation and implementation of future programs and projects, in terms of: Operationalizing the nexus; Achieving program outputs and outcomes; Sustaining outcomes and institutionalizing approaches. 5. Approach and methodology The evaluator's offer in response to this tender should include, as part of the technical offer, a methodological proposal that shows how the evaluator will proceed to achieve the evaluation’s objectives, to make the evaluation useful and to present results that meet high quality standards. The evaluator will favour participatory methods wherever possible. The teams in Ethiopia suggest a combination of a theory-based approach (using comparative case studies) and outcome harvesting. The methodological proposal will contain : A preliminary evaluability assessment , which should demonstrate the main conditions and limitations that the evaluation will face in achieving the planned objectives and in finding answers to the questions posed. It will also indicate how evaluability problems can be solved; The general theoretical-methodological approach that will guide the final evaluation ; A proposal for accompanying the documentation process (case studies) that the project teams will engage in themselves in complement to the final evaluation and for integrating that documentation in the approach and conduct of the final evaluation itself; A proposal for an analytical framework/evaluation matrix for the external evaluation, including evaluation questions, evaluation criteria, means, and sources of information. This matrix is a tool for the implementation of the evaluation questions, but does not replace the theoretical-methodological approach that will guide the evaluation and that should be presented in a clear and differentiated way in the proposal; A description of the evaluation techniques and tools that will be used to collect, classify, analyse and present the required data . The use and analysis of existing and accessible quantitative data is expected. The use of quantitative methods requiring the collection of primary data by the evaluator is not requested. The following sources of information will be made available to the evaluator (list not exhaustive): The theory of change and the program proposal including the results framework; Baseline survey report; Internal narrative annual reports, performance scores and lessons learned (2023-2025, and draft documents for 2026); Monitoring data collected and reports produced by the implementing partners; Resource persons at the level of CI.be and implementing partners. Other documents can be provided upon the evaluator’s request (e.g. concerning meetings, trainings, etc., organised within the framework of the program). 6. Coordination of the evaluation The final evaluation will be coordinated by CI.be’s regional program manager based in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia desk in Brussels, with the support of CI.be’s MEAL officer. The regional program manager and desk officer will be first points of contact of the evaluator, with whom meetings will take place at least at certain specific moments of the process: initial briefing, finalisation of the terms of reference and framing note, discussion of the detailed methodological approach, etc. The regional program manager and desk officer will be responsible for monitoring, accompanying and facilitating the final evaluation process, and more concretely for: Facilitating the evaluator’s access to relevant sources of information (documentation, data, people); Facilitating communication between the evaluator, program implementation teams and partners, and other stakeholders; Monitoring and quality assurance of the process. The formulation of these terms of reference relied on an ongoing consultative process with the implementing partners ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad throughout the program. They will also be consulted during the final evaluation at appropriate times (framing note, draft evaluation report, etc.). Logistics of the evaluation will be coordinated by the regional program manager and ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad. 7. Reports and feedback Nature of the documents to be delivered According to a timetable agreed at the start of the evaluation and in accordance with § 8.2, the evaluator will provide the following documents and reports: A methodological “framing note” specifying the approach and methods that will be used by the evaluator to collect the required data and information; A provisional evaluation report presented for discussion and comment to CI.be and the implementing partners; A final evaluation report taking into account the remarks made on the provisional report and/or adding in annex the collection of comments not taken into account, accompanied by the reasons for not doing so. Quality of the documents Reports should be understandable and easy to read. The results and analyses must be detailed. Causal links between findings, conclusions and recommendations should be clearly visible and sequences of reasoning clearly expressed. Conclusions and recommendations should be well argued and usable in an optimal way by the final evaluation’s stakeholders (CI.be and partners, DGD, other stakeholders, ...). It is therefore important that the recommendations are limited in number number and presented in order of priority and that they are operational in order to facilitate CI.be’s and partners’ management responses. Where relevant, different options available can be explored as well as risks and limitations associated with each option. Structure of the final report Table of contents ; List of abbreviations and acronyms; Executive summary (maximum 1 page, including main findings and recommendations, with interpretation); Key information on the program and the methodology used; Well-argued findings on the evaluation questions and DAC criteria (analysing the collected and accessed data); Conclusions and recommendations, including a synthetic table presenting findings – recommendations – targeted actor (maximum 4 pages); Annexes: Terms of Reference; implemented work program (activities, list of people and organizations met, …); list of documentation consulted; inventory and documentation of lessons learned; comments not taken into account, with reasons for not taking them into account. Even though the inventory and documentation of lessons learned is presented in an annex, it should be treated as of equal importance to the main report. 8. Practical aspects 8.1 The process Phase 1: framing the assignment The evaluator will finalise the methodological approach proposed in their offer on the basis of initial briefings by CI.be and a first reading of the documents (as mentioned in § 5) shared with them. The documentation will be made available to the evaluator at the start of their work. This stage will be an opportunity for the evaluator and CI.be and its partners to conclude possible refining of the evaluation questions presented in § 4. Phase 2: documentation through case studies The partners and implementation teams in Eastern Tigray and Wolaita can engage in case studies, intended to complement the documentation process and to support the external evaluation. CI.be encourages that such case studies are organized, while being accompanied methodologically by the evaluator, who then monitors and validates the process and its relevance for the final evaluation. Phase 3: desk study and preparation of field visit During this phase, the main stakeholders involved in the field visit will be identified. The evaluator will interview online or in-person key staff of CI.be at head office and regional office, read the available documentation and develop a methodological approach (including a timetable, persons and/or groups to be met and organisation of first local feedback meeting/workshop). Phase 4: field visit The fieldwork will concern only the action in Wolaita, given the uncertain security situation in Eastern Tigray. Primary data collection will take into account budget constraints as well as the existence of particular implementation problems, etc. It will focus on those locations and key persons that are considered most relevant in assessing the three methodological innovations in the nexus approach. Sufficient time needs to be planned for methodological briefing and participatory analysis involving the implementation team and stakeholders in Wolaita. The field visit should enable triangulation of the information obtained from the reading and analysis of the documentation of the action with primary data and participatory analysis and sense making with the program teams of the two partner organizations and CI.be’s regional program manager. To allow the Eastern Tigray project team’s involvement in this sense making, they will be invited to participate in the feedback workshop to be organized in Wolaita (to the extent that the budget allows). Phase 5 : data analysis, reporting, presentation and feedback The evaluator will analyse the collected data and produce a draft report, to be presented and discussed at an online feedback session, in which CI.be, ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad will participate. Taking into account these discussions, the evaluator will finalise the evaluation report. S/he will be free to take the comments into consideration or not. However, the remarks which s/he does not take into account must be included in an annex, together with the justification for not taking them into account. In addition, the evaluator is expected to present and participate in an online sensemaking meeting with the program teams of all 7 country programs. The evaluation plan calls for findings and relevant actions to be shared and analysed among country program teams in order to be appropriately leveraged and ensure a collective, horizontal learning process. 8.2 Available budget COHERENCE Ethiopia has foreseen a budget of € 15,000 for its final evaluation, which the offer should not exceed. The amount is understood to be exclusive of expenses related to mobilization of target groups, fieldwork logistics, etc. Otherwise, the tender must include all costs associated with carrying out the assignment: fees, travel expenses, daily allowances, insurance, reproduction costs and any other expenses. The financial offer is deemed to be firm and final. The successful contractor must include in their tender a detailed work plan setting out the number of days worked per activity and per member of the evaluation team, as well as indicative dates and locations. This work plan will be discussed and approved as part of the methodological framing note. The payment terms are as follows: 30 per cent on signing the contract, 40 per cent upon submission of the draft report, and 30 per cent upon approval of the final report. 8.3 Calendar Indicative calendar: Tender: 09/2026 Analysis of offers: 09/2026 Decision on contract: 10/2026 Briefing: 10/2026 Methodological framing note: 10/2026 Documentation process by partners: 10/2026 - 11/2026 Desk study: 10/2026 - 11/2026 Field visit :11/2026 - 12/2026 Draft reporting and feedback: 12/2026 - 01/2027 Final report: 01/2027 Management response: 01/2027 Sharing of report: 02/2027 Multi-country sense making meeting: 12/2026 - 01/2027 8.4 Profile of the evaluator The evaluation should preferably be carried out by a mixed team of consultants. CI.be encourages gender balance among applicants. Required expertise and experience: Program design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, including outcome harvesting; Organisation of participatory evaluations; Capacity building of grassroots institutions and empowerment; Technical expertise areas: HDP nexus and conflict-sensitive development; Gender equity and empowerment; Agroecology; Social cohesion and peacebuilding (small p); Rural development and social technology innovation; Proficiency in "results-based management" and "theory of change" methods; Geographical experience in Ethiopia and knowledge of the local context (Wolaita, Eastern Tigray); Knowledge of local languages. The CVs of the evaluator and their team proposed for this evaluation must be attached to the technical and financial offer. 8.5 Selection of the evaluator Tenders will be evaluated on the basis of the quality of the technical offer (80%) and the price of the services offered (20%). The technical offer will be evaluated on the basis of: The methodological approach and understanding of the terms of reference; The proposed approach to the practical organisation of the evaluation (indicative timetable of the different phases); The qualifications and experience in the different fields mentioned above of the expert and team members proposed for the evaluation. For the technical offer, the tenderer must obtain 60% of the points relating to this criterion. If not, the bid will be disregarded. The financial offer (20%) will be evaluated on the basis of: The overall package price (10%); the score (NPX) for the price of offer X will be calculated as follows: NPX = 10 x (lowest bid price)/(bid price X); The average price for a day's service (10%); the score (NPMX) for the average price for a day's service of offer X will be calculated as follows: NPMX = 10 x (lowest average price)/(average price of offer X). The average price per day of service will be calculated by dividing the sum of salary/per diem/accommodation for the evaluation team by the number of days of service offered. All bidders commit to not having any conflict of interest in relation to the program to be evaluated, including in its preparatory phases. 9. Transparency, confidentiality, ethical standards and data ownership 9.1 Transparency and confidentiality The reports to be published will not contain any information that could endanger partners, teams or any other stakeholder, compromise the integrity of the program in any way, or pose any other risk in terms of confidentiality, particularly with regard to the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. The evaluator is required to respect the confidential nature of all documents and data to which they have access during the evaluation process. The results of the evaluation are intended to be made public, in the interest of accountability to the donor and external stakeholders. 9.2 Ethics The evaluator carries out their work in accordance with the quality standards and ethical principles customary in the evaluation sector, including independence of judgement, impartiality, transparency of methods, reporting of findings to those concerned, and respect for the dignity of the people interviewed. The free and informed consent of interviewees is obtained prior to any interview or focus group discussion. Participants are informed of the purpose of the evaluation, how their comments will be used, and their right to refuse answering or to withdraw at any time. Comments reported in the final report are anonymised, unless the persons concerned have given their explicit written consent. Particular attention is paid to the protection of vulnerable individuals. The evaluation team shall immediately report to CI.be any situation brought to its attention that could constitute a breach of personal integrity. 9.3 Conflict of interest Candidates shall declare, in their tender, that there is no conflict of interest, whether actual or apparent, with CI.be, ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad or the donor. In particular, a conflict of interest is deemed to exist where a person has designed, implemented or evaluated all or part of the intervention that is the subject of this evaluation, or where they have a contractual, financial or personal relationship that could compromise the independence of their judgement. Any conflict of interest arising in the course of the assignment must be reported without delay. The concealment of a conflict of interest constitutes grounds for termination of the contract. 9.4 Ownership and retention of data All data collected, transcripts, recordings, field notes, databases and deliverables produced in the course of the assignment are the exclusive property of Caritas International. The evaluator may not publish, disseminate or reuse all or part of these materials for any other purpose, nor transfer them to third parties, without prior written authorisation of the commissioning bodies. Personal data shall be processed in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation, stored securely for the duration of the assignment and destroyed, or handed over to the commissioning parties, no later than 1 month after the final report has been approved. A certificate of destruction shall be provided.

How to Apply: Interested candidates are invited to submit a technical proposal and a financial proposal. Proposals must not exceed 10 pages, excluding any attached CVs. To secure reliable transportation services for staff coordinating and supporting the implementation of the NbS4Water Africa – Ethiopia Awash Project Background Project Reference: - Donor reference: DN01983 About IUCN IUCN is a membership Union uniquely composed of both government and civil society organisations. It provides public, private and non-governmental organisations with the knowledge and tools that enable human progress, economic development and nature conservation to take place together. Created in 1948, IUCN is now the world’s largest and most diverse environmental network, harnessing the knowledge, resources and reach of more than 1,400 Member organisations and around 15,000 experts. It is a leading provider of conservation data, assessments and analysis. Its broad membership enables IUCN to fill the role of incubator and trusted repository of best practices, tools and international standards. IUCN provides a neutral space in which diverse stakeholders including governments, NGOs, scientists, businesses, local communities, indigenous peoples organisations and others can work together to forge and implement solutions to environmental challenges and achieve sustainable development. Working with many partners and supporters, IUCN implements a large and diverse portfolio of conservation projects worldwide. Combining the latest science with the traditional knowledge of local communities, these projects work to reverse habitat loss, restore ecosystems and improve people’s well-being. www.iucn.org https://twitter.com/IUCN/ About the Project The project focuses on promoting catchment protection through Nature-based Solutions (NbS), framed as best adaptive practices in the context of climate change and increasing land degradation. It aims to scale up NbS for watershed restoration in alignment with national basin development, land degradation neutrality, and landscape restoration goals. The general objective is to enhance water-related ecosystem services in key watersheds of the Awash sub-basin for the benefit of both people and the environment through the application of NbS.
